text: The Radical Civic Union (Unión Cívica Radical, UCR) is a major political party in Argentina and the second oldest active political party in the country, founded in 1891 by Leandro N. Alem. It has held the national government on ten occasions and is one of the most historically significant parties in Argentina. Ideologically, the UCR has stood for radicalism, secularism, and universal suffrage, with a strong advocacy for human rights, especially during the 1970s and 1980s. The party's factions have ranged from conservative liberalism to social democracy, and it has been described as a centrist, liberal, big tent, or catch-all party, with some identifying it as social-liberal or social-democratic. The term "radical" in its name referred to its demand for universal male suffrage, which was considered radical at the time due to Argentina's oligarchic governance. The UCR split from the Civic Union, led by Bartolomé Mitre and Leandro Alem, after hardliners opposed a compromise with President Miguel Juárez Celman during the Revolution of the Park in 1893. The party led further attempts to overthrow the government in 1893 and 1905. In 1912, the UCR helped pass the Sáenz Peña Law, which introduced free, fair, and confidential voting based on universal adult male suffrage, enabling the party to win the 1916 general election and elect Hipólito Yrigoyen as president. Yrigoyen's presidency, though promising popular participation and tackling social problems, was marked by authoritarian tendencies, including refusal to cooperate with Congress. The UCR remained in power until 1930, when a military coup ousted Yrigoyen amid a depression-era economic crisis. From 1930 to 1958, the party was the main opposition, either to Conservatives and the military or to Peronists. In 1958, a faction of the UCR allied with banned Peronists to return to power under Arturo Frondizi, whose tolerance of Peronist allies provoked unrest, leading to his ousting in 1962. In 1963, Arturo Illia won the presidency with 25% of the vote, though only 19% of Peronist votes were blank due to the party's ban, and his administration ended in 1966 when the army removed him. During the 1970s, the UCR was the second-most supported party under Peronist rule, but the rivalry with Peronism ended when leader Ricardo Balbín saluted Perón's coffin with the statement "This old adversary salutes a great friend," marking a shift in political dynamics. The military coup of 1976 ended Peronist rule, and during the military regime, many UCR members were "disappeared." Between 1983 and 1989, Raúl Alfonsín, the UCR's leader, became the first democratically elected president after the military dictatorship, campaigning for clean government and civil rights, representing a fundamental shift toward genuine democracy. In 1997, the UCR ran in coalition with FREPASO, leading to Fernando de la Rúa's election in 1999. De la Rúa resigned in 2001 amid economic turmoil and riots, leading to a succession of acting presidents before Eduardo Duhalde took office. After the 2001 legislative elections, the UCR became the second-largest party in the Chamber of Deputies with 71 seats. Its 2003 presidential candidate, Leopoldo Moreau, received only 2.34% of the vote, losing to three Peronists and two former radicals, Ricardo López Murphy and Elisa Carrió. Since the Peronist Party under Nestor and Cristina Kirchner moved left, the UCR aligned with center-right anti-Peronist parties. In 2005, the UCR had 35 deputies and 13 senators, remaining the second political force. Ahead of the 2007 election, internal divisions emerged between those wanting an internal candidate and those supporting Roberto Lavagna. In May 2005, the National Committee suspended the Tierra del Fuego Provincial Committee after its governor supported Kirchner's reelection, a move rejected by the provincial committee. In August 2006, a party convention in Rosario rejected alliances with Kirchner's faction and allowed former president Roberto Iglesias to negotiate with other forces, leading to talks with Lavagna. In November 2006, the Mendoza Provincial Committee was intervened due to support for Kirchner by Governor Julio Cobos, though the decision was overturned by the provincial electoral justice. Deputy Margarita Stolbizer stated the party was "virtually broken" due to leaders supporting the Kirchner alliance. Iglesias resigned in November 2006, joined Stolbizer's camp, and advocated for a new candidate (Radicales R). On 1 December 2006, Gerardo Morales was appointed party president, stating he would follow the Rosario convention's mandate to pursue an alliance with Lavagna. Morales became Lavagna's running mate in the 2007 presidential election, finishing third. Cobos was elected vice president under Cristina Fernández de Kirchner through the Plural Consensus alliance, and several Radicals entered Congress as part of the Kirchners' Front for Victory. The UCR's official representation in Congress dropped to 30 deputies and 10 senators. Internal disputes over support for Cristina Fernández de Kirchner and Néstor Kirchner persisted, though most Radicales K support ended by mid-2008 when Cobos opposed a government agricultural tax bill. He later rejoined the UCR as a prominent opposition figure. In 2009, the UCR joined the Civic and Social Agreement, which won 29% of the national vote and came second to the Front for Victory. The party reorganized and gained representation in Congress. In 2015, the UCR formed a coalition with Republican Proposal to create Cambiemos, which won the presidential election, ending 12 years of opposition. The alliance with Republican Proposal was criticized by the Socialist International and led to the suspension of the Young Radicals from the International Union of Socialist Youth. Since 2023, the UCR has been in opposition to the Milei administration, agreeing to negotiate individual reform bills. The party is headed by a National Committee, with its president serving as the de facto leader. A national convention brings together provincial representatives and affiliated organizations like Franja Morada and Radical Youth. Raúl Alfonsín believed radicalism advocated social democracy and emphasized that the party defined itself ethically rather than ideologically on a left-right spectrum, viewing itself as observers of European social democracy. In 1995, Alfonsín brought the UCR into the Socialist International. Angel Rozas described the party as humanist and center-left, giving it a progressive orientation. On the conservative side, Ricardo Balbín held influence, and after his death, Fernando de la Rúa introduced neoliberal and conservative policies, famously stating "we are radicals, not socialists." In 1989, Eduardo Angeloz promised a "red pencil" to cut public deficits and mentioned privatization, which was later implemented by Carlos Menem. Since de la Rúa's death in 2001, the UCR has become increasingly fragmented politically and geographically. In 2006, party leaders considered interventions against provincial committees in Río Negro and Santiago del Estero. In Santa Fe, the UCR allied with the Socialist Party to support Hermes Binner for governor, in exchange for the vice-governorship, won by Griselda Tessio. Since the 2005 legislative elections, the UCR has gradually shifted toward center-right positions due to internal divisions and the exclusion of Alfonsinismo, leading to a more conservative orientation. The party now includes a centrist sector and one linked to right-wing values. The UCR ended its political abstention and participated in parliamentary elections with secret ballots, marking a shift from the previous "predictable vote" system, where votes were public and voluntary. The Sáenz Peña Law of 1912 established the secret and obligatory vote, but because it excluded women's suffrage, Argentina did not have a truly universal voting system.

In 1919, the Entinian political party proposed a legal project to grant women the right to vote, but it did not pass due to the conservative majority in Congress. Gabino Ezeiza was a prominent Payador who musically portrayed popular culture in support of Yrigoyen. The UCR ended its electoral abstention and participated in parliamentary elections without forming alliances, marking the first time in Argentina that voters used a voting booth to ensure a secret ballot. Prior to 1912, Argentina employed a system known as the "predictable vote," where votes were expressed verbally or by ticket in public, voluntarily, which undermined the electoral process. The struggle for democracy in Argentina was primarily centered on the introduction of the secret vote in a voting booth, which allowed voters to express their choices independently of external pressures. The Sáenz Peña Law of 1912 established the secret and obligatory vote, yet because it excluded women from voting, it is inaccurate to claim that Argentina had a truly universal suffrage system until 1947. The UCR first achieved electoral success by winning the governorship of Santa Fe (Manuel Menchaca), followed by victories in other regions. Key radical leaders during this period included José Camilo Crotto (CF), Leopoldo Melo (CF), Vicente Gallo (CF), Fernando Saguier (CF), Marcelo T. de Alvear (CF), José L. Cantilo (CF), Delfor del Valle (PBA), Horacio Oyhanarte (PBA), Rogelio Araya (SF), Rodolfo Lehmann (SF), Enrique Mosca (SF), Elpidio González (CBA), Pelagio Luna (LR), Miguel Laurencena (ER), José Néstor Lencinas (Mza), and Federico Cantoni (SJ). The electoral successes of radicalism led to the collapse of parties associated with the pre-Sáenz Peña political system, and the UCR effectively dispersed due to an initiative by Honorio Pueyrredón, with its members joining the radical movement, resulting in the dissolution of the National Autonomist Party. On April 2, 1916, Argentina held its first presidential election by secret ballot, with the UCR securing 370,000 votes compared to 340,000 from all other parties; in the Electoral College, their victory was confirmed. This led to a 14-year cycle of radical government, with the UCR winning three consecutive presidential elections: Hipólito Yrigoyen (1916–1922), Marcelo T. de Alvear (1922–1928), and Hipólito Yrigoyen again (1928–1930). This period of radical rule was abruptly ended by a military coup on December 6, 1930. The secret vote marked a significant turning point in Argentine history. The UCR government included members of previously excluded medial sectors in state leadership roles. Yrigoyen’s first presidency introduced a new type of politics, signaling a transformative nationalist trend, including the creation of YPF (state-owned oil company), new rural laws, strengthening public railways, the Reform University, and a more autonomous foreign policy. On labor issues, Yrigoyen enacted laws such as the eight-hour workday and Sunday rest, and acted as a neutral mediator between labor unions and large companies. However, during his administration, major worker massacres occurred, including the Tragic Week, the La Forestral massacre, and the Firing Squad Executions of Patagonia, resulting in thousands of deaths. Historian Halperín Donghi notes that while radical governments addressed regional equality in Argentina, they simultaneously increased social inequalities due to their lack of solutions for the lower social classes, as they systematically ignored class differences. During Yrigoyen’s first term, radicalism was a minority in Congress: 45 radicals versus 70 opponents in the Chamber of Deputies, and 4 radicals among 30 senators. Nevertheless, Yrigoyen maintained an anti-accord stance and engaged in inflammatory negotiations, both with conservative parties controlling the Senate and with emerging popular parties—such as the Socialist Party and the Democratic Progressive Party—that gained influence through the secret ballot. He also promoted a system of direct intervention in the provinces and a personal, hands-on style of governance, which drew strong criticism from both within and outside the UCR, labeled as "personalism."
